title: T1102.001 — Web Service - Dead Drop Resolver
subtitle: Watch the full dead drop life cycle: staging, posting, polling, decoding, C2 connection, rotation, and the SOC response.
aria: T1102.001 - Web Service - Dead Drop Resolver

steps.title: Defender view
steps.caption: Stage the hidden server The attacker rents a small server and installs C2 software. The victim does not talk to it yet, and the address does not appear in the malware. Nothing to detect. This happens outside your network, before your logs show anything
steps.defender: WAF, reverse-proxy and application logs record the request, payload and backend behavior.

steps.title: Defender view
steps.caption: Post the dead drop The attacker encodes the C2 address into a blob and posts it to a public paste site or file host. The public raw URL becomes the dead drop that the malware will visit. Nothing in your logs yet. Only the attacker and the public service are involved
steps.defender: WAF, reverse-proxy and application logs record the request, payload and backend behavior.

steps.title: Defender view
steps.caption: Poll on a schedule The infected host fetches the raw URL on a fixed schedule, for example every 30 minutes. The request looks like ordinary web traffic from a normal client. The proxy shows periodic GETs to a paste or file host. A small upload is followed by a larger download, and the process is often not a browser
steps.defender: WAF, reverse-proxy and application logs record the request, payload and backend behavior.

steps.title: Defender view
steps.caption: Decode the blob The malware decodes the blob in memory. The hidden C2 domain or IP appears. Everything happens inside the victim host, so there is no network record of the decode itself. Hard to see directly. EDR may show a short burst of activity in the loader process right before the next connection
steps.defender: WAF, reverse-proxy and application logs record the request, payload and backend behavior.

steps.caption: Call home to the real C2 The malware opens an encrypted connection to the resolved server. The operator now has a live session and can send commands. This is the clearest evidence: a fresh outbound connection to a new IP or domain, seconds after the paste fetch

steps.title: Defender view
steps.caption: Burn and rotate Defenders block the C2 server. The attacker notices, posts a new paste with a fresh C2 address, and lets the old server die. The malware never needed an update. Watch the paste host: same host, new paste ID. The URL changed but the pattern did not
steps.defender: WAF, reverse-proxy and application logs record the request, payload and backend behavior.

steps.title: Defender view
steps.caption: Re-resolve and switch On the next poll the malware decodes the new blob and switches to the fresh server. The channel moves with no user-visible event. This is why dead drops are so resilient. The pattern repeats with a different destination IP. Correlation across the two events is your strongest signal
steps.defender: WAF, reverse-proxy and application logs record the request, payload and backend behavior.

steps.title: Defender view
steps.caption: SOC review, block, and hunt The SOC correlates proxy and firewall data: a paste fetch followed by a new-IP connection within a minute. The analyst blocks the C2, deploys a detection, and hunts for other hosts that did the same. Turn the pattern into a durable rule (Section 5.5), then hunt estate-wide for the same paste IDs and fetch-then-connect timing
